text:
The fog that morning did not merely obscure; it consumed. It was a thick, woolen shroud that swallowed the horizon whole, erasing the line between sea and sky. Elias, keeper of forty years, stood at the gallery rail, his knuckles white against the cold iron. The usual rhythm of the waves had vanished, replaced by a suffocating silence that pressed against his eardrums.

Then, he saw it. Not a ship, nor a bird, but a fracture in the gray. A vertical seam of iridescent violet pulsed gently within the mist, defying the natural order of light. It hovered just above the churning water, steady as a heartbeat. Elias squinted, expecting the trick of exhaustion or the onset of cataracts to claim him. But the color remained, sharp and impossible, casting long, unnatural shadows on the wet stone beneath.

He reached for the logbook, his pen trembling. What do you write when the world breaks its own rules? He recorded the time, the coordinates, and the hue. As he lifted his gaze again, the violet seam widened, revealing not darkness beyond, but a faint, golden sunrise where no sun should be. The lighthouse beam swept past, indifferent and blind, while Elias watched the dawn arrive from the wrong direction, terrified and utterly awake.
